source: agent-written from the MANIT 2025-26 syllabus and the standard first-year texts (Jain and Jain, Dara and Umare); importance is an ESTIMATE until past papers are imported
exam_notes: Papers are usually set as short define/differentiate questions (2-3 marks), 'explain with a neat diagram' questions (5 marks) and numericals on calorific value (Dulong, bomb calorimeter), coal analysis and water hardness/softening. The mini test (10) typically covers one unit, the mid term (20, 1 hour) the first units, and the end term (40, 2 hours) the whole syllabus with at least one numerical. Write formulas with units and draw the apparatus wherever the question says 'describe'.

topics.why: Usually the opening 2-mark line of a lubrication answer ('define lubricant, why is it needed'); rarely a question on its own.
key_points: Friction = resistance to relative motion of two surfaces in contact, due to interlocking/welding of asperities.
Coefficient of friction $\mu = F/N$ (frictional force / normal load).
Harmful effects: wear, heat generation, seizure/welding, energy loss, noise, reduced efficiency.
Useful friction: brakes, belts, clutches, walking, nuts and bolts holding.
Lubricant: a substance introduced between moving surfaces to reduce friction and wear.
Lubrication replaces solid (dry) friction by the fluid (internal) friction of the lubricant.
traps: Saying friction is always harmful: examiners like the line that some friction is essential (brakes, belts).
Confusing 'lubricant' (the substance) with 'lubrication' (the process).
topics.asked_as: 'Define lubricant and lubrication. What are the harmful effects of friction?' (2-3 marks), or as the first part of a 5-mark question on mechanism of lubrication.

questions.q: Define a lubricant. Why is lubrication necessary in machines?
questions.a:
A **lubricant** is a substance introduced between two moving or sliding surfaces to reduce the friction between them.

Lubrication is necessary because friction between moving parts causes (i) wear and tear of the surfaces, (ii) generation of heat which can cause expansion, seizure and local welding, (iii) loss of energy and hence lower efficiency, and (iv) noise. A lubricant keeps the surfaces apart, so these effects are reduced.

questions.q: List four harmful effects of friction between moving machine parts.
questions.a:
1. Wear and tear of the surfaces (loss of dimensions, early failure).
2. Heat generation, causing expansion, seizure or welding of parts.
3. Loss of power/energy, lowering machine efficiency.
4. Noise and vibration.

questions.q: Give two situations where friction is useful, and explain why a lubricant would be wrong there.
questions.a:
1. **Brakes**: braking works by friction between the brake shoe/pad and drum/disc; a lubricant would make the brakes fail.
2. **Belt drives / clutches**: power is transmitted by friction between belt and pulley or clutch plates; a lubricant causes slipping and loss of drive.

So lubricants are used only where relative motion should occur with minimum resistance.

questions.q: Explain, in terms of asperities, why two 'smooth' metal surfaces still show friction.
questions.a: No machined surface is perfectly smooth; under magnification it has peaks and valleys called **asperities**. When two surfaces are pressed together they touch only at the tips of asperities, where the local pressure is very high. The asperities interlock and may cold-weld momentarily. Sliding requires shearing these junctions and lifting over the peaks, and this resistance is friction. A lubricant fills the valleys and separates the peaks, so the shear occurs inside the lubricant instead.

questions.q: The primary purpose of a lubricant is to:
options: Increase the load-carrying capacity of a bearing
Reduce friction and wear between moving surfaces
Increase the temperature of moving parts
Seal the machine against dust only
questions.a: A lubricant is defined as a substance that reduces friction (and hence wear and heat) between moving surfaces. Sealing and cooling are secondary functions.

questions.q: The coefficient of friction is defined as:
questions.a: $\mu = F/N$, the ratio of the frictional force to the normal load; it is dimensionless.

topics.why: A safe 2-3 mark 'list the functions' question that appears regularly in mini tests.
topics.gist:
Reducing friction is the headline job of a lubricant, but a good answer lists all its functions, because each one explains a property tested later in the unit.

A lubricant:
1. **Reduces friction** by keeping surfaces apart, so less power is wasted.
2. **Reduces wear and tear**, so parts last longer and keep their dimensions.
3. **Acts as a coolant**: it carries away the heat produced, preventing expansion and seizure.
4. **Reduces maintenance and running cost**.
5. **Prevents corrosion**, because the film keeps air and moisture off the metal.
6. **Acts as a seal**, e.g. between piston rings and cylinder in an IC engine, preventing leakage of gases.
7. **Reduces noise** and vibration.
8. **Removes dirt and wear debris** (flushing), keeping the working parts clean.
9. **Transmits fluid pressure** in hydraulic systems.

When you write this, number the points and add a few words of explanation to each; a bare list of single words gets fewer marks.
key_points: Reduces friction and hence power loss (improves efficiency).
Reduces wear and tear of moving parts.
Acts as a coolant: removes frictional heat, prevents expansion and seizure.
Prevents corrosion by excluding air and moisture.
Acts as a seal (piston rings in IC engines).
Reduces noise; flushes away dirt and debris.
Reduces running and maintenance costs.
Transmits pressure in hydraulic machines.
traps: Writing only 'reduces friction' for a 3-mark question: list at least five functions.
Forgetting the seal and coolant functions, which are the ones examiners look for after 'reduces friction'.
topics.asked_as: 'What are lubricants? Give their functions.' (2-3 marks); 'Write any four functions of a lubricant' (2 marks).

questions.q: Write any five functions of a lubricant.
questions.a:
1. **Reduces friction** between moving surfaces, so less power is lost and efficiency rises.
2. **Reduces wear and tear** of the surfaces, increasing machine life.
3. **Acts as a coolant**: carries away frictional heat, preventing expansion and seizure.
4. **Prevents corrosion**: the film keeps oxygen and moisture away from the metal.
5. **Acts as a seal**, e.g. between piston and cylinder, preventing leakage of gases.

(Also: reduces noise, flushes away dirt, lowers maintenance cost, transmits pressure in hydraulic systems.)

questions.q: How does a lubricant act as a coolant and as a seal in an IC engine?
questions.a:
**Coolant**: frictional heat generated between piston and cylinder is absorbed by the circulating oil and carried to the sump/oil cooler, so the parts do not expand and seize.

**Seal**: the thin oil film between the piston rings and the cylinder wall fills the clearance, so the compressed gases and combustion gases cannot leak past the piston (better compression, less blow-by).

questions.q: Why does lubrication reduce the running cost of a machine?
questions.a: Because (i) less energy is wasted against friction, so fuel/power consumption falls; (ii) wear is reduced, so parts need replacement less often; (iii) seizure and breakdowns are avoided, reducing downtime and maintenance cost.

questions.q: Name a machine where the lubricant is used mainly to transmit pressure, and name the type of oil used.
questions.a: **Hydraulic systems** (hydraulic presses, brakes, jacks, earth-moving equipment). Hydraulic oils, usually refined mineral oils (or synthetic fluids) with high viscosity index, are used so that the pressure is transmitted uniformly over a range of temperatures.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of a lubricant?
questions.a: A lubricant removes frictional heat; it never increases it. The other three are standard functions.

questions.q: In an IC engine, the lubricant film between piston rings and cylinder wall mainly acts as a:
questions.a: The oil film fills the clearance and prevents leakage (blow-by) of the compressed gases, i.e. it acts as a seal, besides reducing friction.

topics.topic: Mechanisms of lubrication: thick layer, thin layer, extreme pressure
topics.why: The standard 5-mark 'explain the mechanisms of lubrication with diagrams' question of this unit; very likely in mid and end term.
topics.gist:
There are three mechanisms, chosen by load, speed and temperature.

**1. Thick film (fluid film, hydrodynamic) lubrication.** The moving surfaces are completely separated by a film of lubricant at least about $1000\,\mathring{A}$ thick, thicker than the height of the asperities. There is no metal contact; the only resistance is the internal friction (**viscosity**) of the oil. It applies at low load and high speed, e.g. a shaft running in a journal bearing, which drags oil into a wedge and lifts itself. Lubricant: hydrocarbon (mineral) oils of correct viscosity, with anti-oxidants.

**2. Thin film (boundary) lubrication.** At high load, low speed or when oil viscosity is too low, a full film cannot form; the asperities nearly touch. A layer only a few molecules thick is held on the metal by **adsorption** (physical or chemical). The property that matters is **oiliness**, not viscosity. Examples: gears, cams, rail wheels, starting/stopping of machines. Lubricants: vegetable/animal oils, their soaps, fatty acids, graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$.

**3. Extreme pressure lubrication.** Under very high loads and speeds the local temperature is so high that even boundary films desorb or the oil decomposes. **EP additives** (chlorinated esters, sulphurised oils, tricresyl phosphate) react with the hot metal surface to form metal chlorides, sulphides or phosphides. These form a durable, high-melting film that shears easily and prevents welding.
key_points: Thick film: complete separation, film thicker than asperities (~1000 Å); friction only from viscosity; low load, high speed; e.g. journal bearings; mineral oils.
Thin film/boundary: film a few molecules thick held by adsorption; oiliness decides; high load, low speed, start-stop; e.g. gears, cams.
Boundary lubricants: vegetable and animal oils (long-chain polar molecules), fatty acids, graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$.
Extreme pressure: very high load/temperature; EP additives react chemically with metal.
EP additives: chlorinated esters, sulphurised oils, tricresyl phosphate → $\mathrm{FeCl_2}$/$\mathrm{FeCl_3}$, FeS, $\mathrm{FePO_4}$ films.
These metal compound films have high melting points and low shear strength, preventing seizure/welding.
Diagram expected: two surfaces with asperities, separated fully (thick), touching through a molecular layer (thin).
traps: Saying viscosity is what matters in boundary lubrication: it is oiliness (adsorption of polar molecules).
Giving thick-film conditions as 'high load': thick film needs low load and high speed.
Calling EP films 'physically adsorbed': they are chemical reaction products with the metal.
No diagram in a 5-mark answer costs marks; draw two rough surfaces with the film between.
topics.asked_as: 'Explain the mechanism of lubrication with suitable diagrams' (5 marks); 'Differentiate fluid film and boundary lubrication' (3 marks); 'What are EP additives? How do they act?' (2-3 marks).

questions.q: Explain thick film (hydrodynamic) lubrication. Under what conditions does it occur and what lubricants are used?
questions.a:
In **thick film lubrication** the two moving surfaces are completely separated by a continuous film of lubricant whose thickness (about $1000\,\mathring{A}$ or more) exceeds the height of the surface irregularities. Hence there is no direct metal-to-metal contact; the only resistance to motion is the internal friction (viscosity) of the lubricant.

*Conditions*: low load, high speed, e.g. a shaft rotating in a well-fitted journal bearing; the rotating shaft drags oil into the converging gap and builds up pressure that lifts the shaft.

*Diagram*: two rough surfaces with a thick oil layer filling all the space between them, no peaks touching.

*Lubricants*: hydrocarbon (mineral) oils of suitable viscosity; long-chain hydrocarbons blended with anti-oxidants and (for wide temperature range) VI improvers.

*Coefficient of friction*: very low, about 0.001-0.03.

questions.q: Differentiate between thick film and thin film (boundary) lubrication.
questions.a:
| Thick film (hydrodynamic) | Thin film (boundary) |
|---|---|
| Surfaces fully separated by a thick film (>~1000 Å) | Film only a few molecules thick; asperities nearly touch |
| Low load, high speed | High load, low speed, start-stop, low-viscosity oil |
| Friction governed by **viscosity** | Governed by **oiliness** (adsorption on metal) |
| Mineral (hydrocarbon) oils | Vegetable/animal oils, fatty acids, graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ |
| Example: journal bearings | Example: gears, cams, rail axles |

questions.q: What is extreme pressure lubrication? Name three EP additives and explain how they work.
questions.a:
Under very heavy loads and high speeds, the local temperature at the contact is so high that liquid films evaporate or decompose and boundary films desorb, so metal welding can occur. **Extreme pressure lubrication** uses special additives that react with the metal surface.

EP additives: (i) chlorinated esters, (ii) sulphurised oils, (iii) tricresyl phosphate.

At the high surface temperature they react with the metal to form metallic chlorides, sulphides or phosphides (e.g. $\mathrm{FeCl_2}$, $\mathrm{FeS}$, $\mathrm{FePO_4}$) as a thin surface layer. These compounds have high melting points and low shear strength, so the surfaces slide over this layer instead of welding together.

questions.q: Why are vegetable and animal oils good boundary lubricants?
questions.a: Their molecules (triglycerides and free fatty acids) have **polar groups** (-COOH, ester) at one end and long hydrocarbon chains at the other. The polar end is strongly adsorbed on the metal surface and the chains stand side by side like a carpet, forming a strong, oriented film a few molecules thick. This gives high **oiliness**, so the film survives high load where the oil cannot maintain a thick film.

questions.q: In boundary lubrication, the property of the lubricant that matters most is:
questions.a: In boundary lubrication the film is only a few molecules thick and is held by adsorption, so **oiliness** (the ability to stick to the metal) governs performance, not viscosity.

questions.q: Tricresyl phosphate is added to lubricants as a(n):
questions.a: Tricresyl phosphate reacts with the hot metal surface to form a metal phosphide/phosphate film, so it is an **EP additive**.

questions.q: Thick film lubrication is favoured by:
questions.a: A full hydrodynamic film builds up when the speed is high enough to drag oil into the gap and the load is low enough not to squeeze it out.

topics.why: Greases and solid lubricants (graphite vs $\mathrm{MoS_2}$) are frequent 3-5 mark short notes; classification is a 2-marker.
topics.gist:
Lubricants are classified by physical state.

**Liquid lubricants (lubricating oils)**: (i) animal and vegetable oils (castor, palm, olive, coconut, tallow, whale oil) have good oiliness but oxidise, become gummy and are costly; (ii) **mineral (petroleum) oils**, obtained from fractional distillation of crude, cheap and stable but poor in oiliness; (iii) **blended oils**: mineral oil plus additives (oiliness agents, anti-oxidants, VI improvers, pour-point depressants, EP agents); (iv) synthetic oils (silicones, polyglycols) for extreme temperatures.

**Semi-solid lubricants (greases)**: a lubricating oil thickened with a metallic soap. Used where oil cannot stay in place: slow speed with high load, intermittent operation, exposed bearings, where dust/moisture must be sealed out. **Calcium-soap (cup) grease**: water-resistant, used below about $80\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$. **Sodium-soap grease**: higher temperatures (about $175\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) but not water-resistant. **Lithium-soap grease**: water-resistant and usable over a wide temperature range. Greases have higher friction than oils and poor cooling.

**Solid lubricants**: used at very high load/temperature, where oil would burn or contaminate (food, textile machines). **Graphite**: layers of hexagonal carbon held by weak van der Waals forces slide over each other; works up to about $500\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ in air, used as powder, in oil (oildag) or water (aquadag). **Molybdenum disulphide** ($\mathrm{MoS_2}$): sandwich layers of S-Mo-S, stable up to about $800\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, works in vacuum. Others: talc, mica, soapstone.
key_points: Three classes: liquid (oils), semi-solid (greases), solid.
Vegetable/animal oils: good oiliness, poor oxidation stability, costly.
Mineral oils: cheap, stable, poor oiliness; improved by blending additives.
Grease = oil + metallic soap thickener (+ fillers).
Ca-soap grease: water-resistant, low temperature; Na-soap: high temperature, not water-resistant; Li-soap: both.
Greases used for slow speed/high load, exposed or intermittently working bearings, sealing against dust.
Graphite: layered structure, weak interlayer van der Waals forces; oildag and aquadag.
$\mathrm{MoS_2}$: layer lattice, stable to higher temperature, works in vacuum.
Solid lubricants used where heavy load, high temperature, or contamination by oil is unacceptable.
traps: Saying sodium greases are water-resistant: they are not (sodium soap is water-soluble); calcium greases are.
Explaining graphite lubrication by 'covalent bonds between layers': the layers are held by weak van der Waals forces.
Mixing up oildag (graphite in oil) and aquadag (graphite in water).
topics.asked_as: 'Write a short note on greases / solid lubricants' (3-5 marks); 'Why is graphite a good lubricant?' (2 marks); 'Classify lubricants with examples' (3 marks).

questions.q: What are greases? Give their composition, types and applications.
questions.a:
**Greases** are semi-solid lubricants made by thickening a lubricating oil (usually mineral oil) with a **metallic soap** (Ca, Na, Li, Al soaps); fillers such as graphite, talc or mica may be added.

**Types**:
- *Calcium-soap (cup) grease*: water-resistant, cheap; used below about 80 °C (water pumps, tractors).
- *Sodium-soap grease*: usable up to about 175 °C but not water-resistant (ball bearings in dry conditions).
- *Lithium-soap grease*: water-resistant and good over a wide temperature range (automobile multipurpose grease).

**Applications**: where oil cannot be retained: slow speed and heavy load bearings, intermittent operation, rail axles, exposed gears, where dust and moisture must be sealed out.

**Limitations**: higher friction than oil and poor heat removal.

questions.q: Explain why graphite is a good solid lubricant. Where are solid lubricants preferred?
questions.a:
Graphite has a **layer structure**: each layer is a sheet of hexagonally linked $sp^2$ carbon atoms, and the layers are about 3.35 Å apart, held only by weak **van der Waals forces**. Under shear the layers slide easily over one another, giving low friction; graphite is also non-inflammable and stable in air up to about 500 °C.

It is used as dry powder, as **oildag** (dispersion in oil) or **aquadag** (in water).

Solid lubricants are preferred where (i) loads are very heavy and speeds low, (ii) temperatures are too high for oils, (iii) oil contamination is unacceptable (food, textile, paper machinery), (iv) access for re-oiling is difficult.

questions.q: Compare graphite and molybdenum disulphide as solid lubricants.
questions.a:
| Graphite | $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ |
|---|---|
| Hexagonal carbon layers held by van der Waals forces | S-Mo-S sandwich layers, weak S-S interlayer forces |
| Usable up to ~500 °C in air | Usable up to ~800 °C |
| Needs adsorbed moisture/vapour to lubricate well; poor in vacuum | Lubricates well in vacuum (space applications) |
| Used as oildag, aquadag, in greases | Used as powder, in greases, bonded coatings |

questions.q: Give two advantages and two disadvantages of vegetable oils compared with mineral oils as lubricants.
questions.a:
*Advantages*: (1) excellent oiliness (polar molecules adsorb on metal), good for boundary lubrication; (2) biodegradable.

*Disadvantages*: (1) poor oxidation stability: they oxidise, become gummy and acidic; (2) costly and they hydrolyse easily in moisture. Hence they are blended in small amounts into mineral oils as oiliness carriers.

questions.q: Which grease is water-resistant but suitable only for relatively low temperatures?
questions.a: Calcium-soap (cup) grease is insoluble in water, hence water-resistant, but it contains water as stabiliser and breaks down above about 80 °C.

questions.q: Aquadag is:
options: A suspension of graphite in water
questions.a: Aquadag is colloidal graphite dispersed in water; oildag is graphite dispersed in oil.

topics.topic: Physical and chemical properties of lubricants and their testing
topics.why: The most examined lubricant topic: definitions with significance (viscosity index, flash/fire, cloud/pour, aniline point) and numericals on VI, acid value and saponification value.
topics.gist:
For each property, learn three things: **definition, how it is measured, and why it matters**.

**Viscosity**: resistance to flow; measured with the **Redwood** viscometer (No. 1 for thin oils, No. 2 for viscous oils; time in seconds for 50 mL to flow) or Saybolt. Too low: film breaks; too high: power loss.
**Viscosity index (VI)**: the rate of change of viscosity with temperature. High VI means viscosity changes little; needed in IC engines. Dean and Davis scale: Pennsylvanian oil = 100, Gulf coast oil = 0.
**Flash point**: lowest temperature at which the oil gives enough vapour to ignite momentarily when a flame is brought near; **fire point**: lowest temperature at which the vapour burns continuously for at least 5 s. Fire point is usually 5-40 °C above flash point. Measured with **Pensky-Martens** (closed cup) or Cleveland (open cup). A good lubricant's flash point is above the working temperature.
**Cloud point / pour point**: temperature at which the oil becomes cloudy (waxes separate) / ceases to flow. Low values needed for cold conditions.
**Aniline point**: lowest temperature at which equal volumes of oil and aniline are completely miscible. High aniline point means few aromatics, so less attack on rubber seals.
**Oiliness**, **carbon residue** (Conradson), **volatility**, **emulsification** (steam emulsion number).

Chemical: **acid value** (mg KOH to neutralise free acids in 1 g oil; should be below about 0.1), **saponification value** (mg KOH to saponify 1 g oil; identifies vegetable/animal oil in a blend; mineral oils do not saponify), **iodine value** (unsaturation; high value means oil oxidises and gums).
key_points: Viscosity: Redwood viscometer No. 1 (thin oils) and No. 2 (viscous oils); result in Redwood seconds.
VI: high VI = small change of viscosity with temperature; Dean and Davis method.
Flash point < fire point; both should exceed operating temperature; Pensky-Martens closed cup apparatus.
Cloud point and pour point: low values needed for oils used in cold weather.
Aniline point: high value means low aromatic content and so less swelling of rubber seals.
Acid value: mg KOH per g of oil for free acid; good oil < 0.1.
Saponification value: mg KOH per g of oil to saponify; detects vegetable/animal oil in mineral oil.
Iodine value: degree of unsaturation; high value = poor oxidation stability.
Carbon residue (Conradson): tendency to deposit carbon in engines; should be low.
Steam emulsion number: time (s) for oil and water emulsion to separate; low value = good demulsibility (turbines).
formulas: $\mathrm{VI} = \dfrac{L-U}{L-H} \times 100$ — Dean and Davis viscosity index (viscosities at 100 °F; L, H at 210 °F equal to U's)
$\text{Saponification value} = \dfrac{(B - S) \times N_{\mathrm{HCl}} \times 56}{W_{\mathrm{oil}}}$ mg KOH/g — B blank, S sample titre
traps: Defining fire point as 'the temperature at which oil catches fire': it is the lowest temperature at which vapours burn continuously for at least 5 seconds.
Using 40 (eq. wt) instead of 56 (molar mass of KOH) in acid/saponification value formulas.
In saponification value, subtracting the wrong way: it is (blank − sample) titre.
Saying a high aniline point is bad: high aniline point means fewer aromatics, which is good for rubber seals.
Mixing up which oil is VI 100 (Pennsylvanian, paraffinic) and VI 0 (Gulf coast, naphthenic).
topics.asked_as: 'Define and give the significance of: viscosity index, flash and fire point, cloud and pour point, aniline point' (2 marks each or 5 together); 'Describe the Redwood viscometer / Pensky-Martens apparatus' (5); numericals on VI, acid value, saponification value (3-5).

questions.q: Define flash point and fire point. Give their significance and name the apparatus used.
questions.a:
**Flash point**: the lowest temperature at which a lubricating oil gives off enough vapours that ignite momentarily (a flash) when a small flame is brought near it.

**Fire point**: the lowest temperature at which the vapours of the oil burn continuously for at least five seconds when a flame is brought near. Fire point is generally 5-40 °C higher than flash point.

**Significance**: a good lubricant must have a flash point well above its working temperature, so that it does not catch fire in use; they also guide safe storage and transport.

**Apparatus**: Pensky-Martens (closed cup) apparatus; Abel's apparatus for low flash oils; Cleveland open cup.

questions.q: Define viscosity index. An oil under test has a kinematic viscosity of 300 cSt at 100 °F. The Gulf coast (L) and Pennsylvanian (H) standard oils having the same viscosity as the test oil at 210 °F have viscosities of 500 cSt and 200 cSt at 100 °F. Calculate the VI.
questions.a:
**Viscosity index** is a number expressing how little the viscosity of an oil changes with temperature; a high VI means the viscosity is nearly constant over a range of temperature.

By Dean and Davis:
$$\mathrm{VI} = \frac{L-U}{L-H}\times 100$$
where $U$ = viscosity of test oil at 100 °F = 300 cSt, $L$ = 500 cSt (Gulf oil, VI 0), $H$ = 200 cSt (Pennsylvanian oil, VI 100).

$$\mathrm{VI} = \frac{500-300}{500-200}\times 100 = \frac{200}{300}\times 100 = 66.7$$

The oil has VI ≈ 67 (moderate).

questions.q: 2.0 g of an oil was saponified with 25 mL of 0.5 N alcoholic KOH. The excess KOH needed 15.0 mL of 0.5 N HCl. A blank (25 mL KOH) needed 25.0 mL of the same HCl. Calculate the saponification value. Is the oil a pure mineral oil?
questions.a:
KOH used for saponification = (blank − sample) titre = 25.0 − 15.0 = 10.0 mL of 0.5 N.

Milliequivalents of KOH = $10.0 \times 0.5 = 5.0$ meq.
Mass of KOH = $5.0 \times 56 = 280$ mg.

$$\text{Saponification value} = \frac{280\ \text{mg}}{2.0\ \text{g}} = 140\ \text{mg KOH/g}$$

Mineral oils are not saponified (saponification value ≈ 0), so this oil is (or contains a large proportion of) vegetable/animal oil.

questions.q: 10 g of a lubricating oil required 2.5 mL of 0.1 N KOH for neutralisation. Find its acid value and comment on its suitability.
questions.a:
mg KOH = $V \times N \times 56 = 2.5 \times 0.1 \times 56 = 14$ mg.

$$\text{Acid value} = \frac{14}{10} = 1.4\ \text{mg KOH/g}$$

A good lubricating oil should have an acid value below about 0.1. Since 1.4 is much higher, the oil contains free acids (oxidation products), which corrode metal parts; it is **unsuitable**.

questions.q: Define cloud point, pour point and aniline point and state the significance of each.
questions.a:
**Cloud point**: the temperature at which an oil, on slow cooling, becomes cloudy or hazy because waxes begin to crystallise.
**Pour point**: the temperature at which the oil just ceases to flow (pour).
*Significance*: oils used in cold climates or refrigeration should have low cloud and pour points, otherwise they will not flow and lubricate.

**Aniline point**: the minimum equilibrium temperature at which equal volumes of aniline and the oil are completely miscible.
*Significance*: aromatics dissolve aniline at low temperature, so a **high aniline point** means a low aromatic content; such oil will not swell or dissolve rubber seals and packings.

questions.q: A lubricant used in an IC engine should have:
options: Low viscosity index and low flash point
High viscosity index and high flash point
questions.a: Engine oils face a wide temperature range (high VI keeps viscosity steady) and high temperatures (high flash point avoids fire). High iodine and acid values are undesirable.

questions.q: Saponification value of a lubricant is used mainly to:
options: Detect vegetable or animal oil in it
questions.a: Only esters (vegetable/animal oils) are saponified by KOH; mineral oils are not, so a non-zero value reveals blended fatty oil.

questions.q: Which apparatus is used for determining the flash point of a lubricating oil?
questions.a: Pensky-Martens (closed cup) apparatus is the standard for flash point; Redwood measures viscosity; bomb and Junkers calorimeters measure calorific value.

topics.why: Occasionally a 2-3 mark short note; rarely a full question.
key_points: Emulsion = oil + water + emulsifying agent.
Oil-in-water emulsions for cooling; water-in-oil for lubrication with some water present.
Cutting fluid functions: cooling, lubrication, prevent chip welding, flush chips, surface finish, corrosion protection.
Soluble oil = mineral oil + emulsifier, diluted with water (milky emulsion).
Straight (neat) cutting oils with EP additives for heavy-duty cuts.
Good cutting fluid: high specific heat/thermal conductivity, non-corrosive, non-toxic, stable, does not foam.
traps: Saying soluble oils are true solutions: they form emulsions.
Listing only 'lubrication': the main function of most cutting fluids is cooling.
topics.asked_as: 'Write a short note on cutting fluids' (3 marks); 'What are lubricating emulsions? Give their types' (2 marks).

questions.q: What are cutting fluids? Give their functions.
questions.a:
**Cutting fluids** are liquids (usually oil-water emulsions or oils) applied at the cutting zone during machining operations.

**Functions**:
1. Cool the cutting tool and workpiece, increasing tool life and maintaining dimensional accuracy.
2. Lubricate the tool-chip and tool-work interfaces, reducing friction and power consumption.
3. Prevent welding of chips to the tool (built-up edge).
4. Wash away chips from the cutting zone.
5. Improve surface finish and protect the machined surface against corrosion.

questions.q: Distinguish between oil-in-water and water-in-oil emulsions as lubricants.
questions.a:
**Oil-in-water**: water is the continuous phase with oil droplets dispersed in it; high cooling capacity; used as soluble cutting oils in machining.

**Water-in-oil**: oil is the continuous phase with water droplets dispersed in it; lubricating action dominates while the water adds some cooling or fire resistance; used in some steam engines, marine and fire-resistant hydraulic fluids.

Both need an emulsifying agent (soaps, sulphonated oils) to remain stable.

questions.q: What is a soluble oil? Why is it widely used in machining?
questions.a: A **soluble oil** is a mineral oil containing an emulsifying agent (soap or sulphonated oil). When mixed with water (typically 1:10 to 1:40) it forms a milky oil-in-water emulsion. It is widely used because the water gives excellent cooling while the oil gives lubrication and rust protection, and it is cheap.

questions.q: Which properties should a good cutting fluid have? (any four)
questions.a:
1. High specific heat and thermal conductivity (good cooling).
2. Good lubricating property (oiliness, EP action for heavy cuts).
3. Non-corrosive to work and machine.
4. Non-toxic and free of bad odour; does not irritate skin.
5. Stable, does not foam or turn rancid; low cost.

questions.q: The main function of a soluble oil emulsion in a lathe operation is:
options: Cooling of the tool and work, with some lubrication
questions.a: The water phase gives cooling, which is the chief need at the tool tip; the oil phase adds lubrication and rust protection.

questions.q: A lubricating emulsion consists of:
options: Oil, water and an emulsifying agent
questions.a: An emulsion is a dispersion of oil and water stabilised by an emulsifying agent such as soap.

topics.topic: Selection of lubricants for light and heavy machinery
topics.why: A common 3-5 mark 'which lubricant would you choose for ... and why' question tying properties to applications.
topics.gist:
Selection follows directly from the mechanism needed and the operating conditions (load, speed, temperature, environment).

**Light machinery and delicate instruments** (watches, clocks, sewing machines, scientific instruments, typewriters): loads are small and speeds moderate; we need a **light (low viscosity)** oil with **high oiliness**, good oxidation resistance and no gumming. Use refined light mineral oil blended with a little vegetable oil, or neatsfoot/clock oil.

**Heavy machinery** (rolling mills, crushers, cranes, heavy gears, rail axles): high load and low speed, so boundary or EP conditions prevail. Use **high-viscosity oils**, **greases**, oils with **EP additives**, or solid lubricants (graphite, $\mathrm{MoS_2}$) where temperature is very high.

Other common cases:
- **IC engines**: high VI, high flash point, low pour point, low carbon residue, with detergent and antioxidant additives (multigrade oils).
- **Steam turbines**: low viscosity, high oxidation stability, **good demulsibility** (low steam emulsion number) because the oil contacts steam.
- **Cutting tools**: cutting fluids (soluble oil emulsions; straight oils with EP for heavy cuts).
- **Transformers**: refined mineral oil of high dielectric strength, free of moisture.
- **Refrigeration**: low pour and cloud point.
- **Food/textile machinery**: solid lubricants or food-grade oils so no staining.
key_points: Selection depends on load, speed, temperature, environment (water, dust, chemicals).
Light machinery: low viscosity, high oiliness, non-gumming, oxidation-resistant oils.
Heavy machinery: high viscosity oils, greases, EP additives, solid lubricants.
IC engines: high VI, high flash point, low pour point, low carbon residue.
Steam turbines: good demulsibility, oxidation stability, high VI.
Transformers: high dielectric strength mineral oil.
Refrigerators: low cloud and pour point.
Delicate instruments/watches: light clock oils, non-volatile.
traps: Giving a heavy grease for a watch, or a light oil for rolling mills: match viscosity to load.
Forgetting demulsibility for steam turbines, which is the property examiners expect.
topics.asked_as: 'Which lubricant would you recommend for (a) watches (b) IC engines (c) steam turbines (d) heavy gears? Justify.' (5 marks); 'Discuss the criteria for selection of lubricants' (5 marks).

questions.q: Suggest suitable lubricants, with reasons, for: (a) delicate instruments and watches, (b) heavy machinery such as rolling mills and crushers.
questions.a:
**(a) Delicate instruments/watches**: loads are very light and parts small. A **light, low-viscosity oil with high oiliness** is needed, which must not gum, oxidise or evaporate. Highly refined light mineral oil blended with a little vegetable/animal oil (e.g. neatsfoot or clock oil) is used.

**(b) Heavy machinery**: high load, low speed and often high temperature, so a thick film cannot be maintained (boundary/extreme pressure conditions). Use **high-viscosity oils with EP additives** (sulphurised/chlorinated compounds), **greases** for slow, heavily loaded bearings, and **solid lubricants** such as graphite or $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ at very high temperature or load.

questions.q: What properties should a lubricant for an IC engine possess?
questions.a:
1. **High viscosity index**: viscosity should stay adequate from cold start to hot running.
2. **High flash and fire points**: the cylinder region is hot.
3. **Low pour point**: for cold starts.
4. **Low carbon residue** and good oxidation stability: no sludge or carbon deposits.
5. Additives: detergents/dispersants, antioxidants, anti-wear agents, pour-point depressants.

questions.q: Why must a steam turbine oil have good demulsibility?
questions.a: In a steam turbine the oil comes into contact with condensed steam (water). If it forms a stable emulsion with water, the lubricating film is lost and sludge forms. Good **demulsibility** (low steam emulsion number) means the oil separates quickly from water, which can then be drained, keeping lubrication effective. Turbine oils also need high oxidation stability.

questions.q: List the factors that govern the choice of a lubricant for a machine.
questions.a:
1. Load on the bearing (light, heavy, shock).
2. Speed of the moving parts.
3. Operating temperature range.
4. Environment: water, steam, dust, chemicals.
5. Type of lubrication regime required (thick film, boundary, EP).
6. Method of application and accessibility.
7. Compatibility with seals/materials and contamination limits (food, textile).
8. Cost and availability.

questions.q: The most suitable lubricant for a transformer is:
options: Refined mineral oil of high dielectric strength
questions.a: Transformer oil must insulate and cool; refined mineral oil with high dielectric strength and no moisture is used.

questions.q: For a lubricant used in refrigeration machinery, the most important properties are:
options: High flash point and high carbon residue
Low cloud point and low pour point
High aniline point and high acid value
questions.a: The oil must stay fluid at very low temperatures, so low cloud and pour points are essential.

topics.topic: Calorific value and characteristics of a good fuel
topics.why: Definitions of calorific value, its units and 'characteristics of a good fuel' are near-certain 2-3 mark questions in the mini and mid tests.
topics.gist:
A **fuel** is a combustible substance containing carbon (and hydrogen) which, on burning in air, gives out heat that can be used economically.

**Calorific value (CV)** is the total quantity of heat liberated when a unit mass (or unit volume, for gases) of a fuel is burnt completely in air or oxygen. It is the single most important figure of merit of a fuel.

**Units**: calorie (heat to raise 1 g water by 1 °C), kilocalorie (1000 cal), British Thermal Unit (BTU, heat to raise 1 lb water by 1 °F), Centigrade Heat Unit (CHU), joule. Common units: cal/g, kcal/kg, BTU/lb, kJ/kg for solids and liquids; kcal/m$^3$ or BTU/ft$^3$ for gases. Note $1\ \text{cal/g} = 1\ \text{kcal/kg} = 1.8\ \text{BTU/lb}$ and $1\ \text{kcal} = 4.184\ \text{kJ}$.

**Characteristics of a good fuel**: high calorific value; moderate **ignition temperature** (too low is a fire hazard, too high is hard to light); low moisture content; low non-combustible matter (ash); moderate velocity of combustion; products of combustion not harmful (little S, N); low cost and easy availability; easy to store and transport; combustion easily controllable; should not burn spontaneously.
key_points: Fuel: carbonaceous combustible substance that gives heat economically on burning.
Calorific value: heat liberated by complete combustion of unit mass/volume of fuel.
Units: cal/g, kcal/kg, BTU/lb, kJ/kg; gases in kcal/m³.
1 kcal/kg = 1 cal/g = 1.8 BTU/lb = 4.184 kJ/kg; 1 BTU = 252 cal.
Ignition temperature: lowest temperature to which fuel must be preheated to burn smoothly; should be moderate.
Good fuel: high CV, moderate ignition temperature, low moisture, low ash, moderate combustion rate, harmless products, cheap, easy to store and transport, controllable combustion.
Classification of fuels: natural (primary) and derived (secondary), each solid, liquid or gas.
traps: Saying a good fuel should have a low ignition temperature: it must be moderate (low is a fire hazard during storage).
Writing 1 kcal/kg = 1000 cal/g: in fact 1 kcal/kg = 1 cal/g.
Forgetting that gaseous fuel CV is per unit volume (at STP).
topics.asked_as: 'Define calorific value. Give its units.' (2 marks); 'What are the characteristics of a good fuel?' (3 marks); 'Classify fuels with examples' (2-3 marks).

questions.q: Define calorific value of a fuel and give its units in different systems.
questions.a:
**Calorific value** of a fuel is the total quantity of heat liberated when a unit mass (or unit volume for a gas) of the fuel is burnt completely in air or oxygen.

**Units**:
- CGS: cal/g
- MKS: kcal/kg
- British: BTU/lb
- SI: J/kg or kJ/kg
- For gases: kcal/m³ (at STP), BTU/ft³

Relations: 1 kcal/kg = 1 cal/g = 1.8 BTU/lb = 4.184 kJ/kg.

questions.q: List the characteristics of a good fuel.
questions.a:
1. High calorific value.
2. Moderate ignition temperature: low enough to light easily, high enough to be safe in storage.
3. Low moisture content (moisture lowers the heating value).
4. Low content of non-combustible matter (ash), which lowers CV and creates disposal problems.
5. Moderate rate of combustion.
6. Combustion products should not be harmful (low S and N).
7. Low cost and readily available.
8. Easy to transport and store.
9. Combustion should be easily controllable (start and stop).
10. Should not undergo spontaneous combustion.

questions.q: Define ignition temperature. Why should it be moderate for a good fuel?
questions.a:
**Ignition temperature** is the lowest temperature to which a fuel must be preheated so that it starts burning smoothly.

If it is too **low**, the fuel can catch fire accidentally during storage and transport (fire hazard). If it is too **high**, the fuel is difficult to kindle. Hence a moderate ignition temperature is desirable.

questions.q: Classify fuels with one example each.
questions.a:
| | Solid | Liquid | Gaseous |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Natural (primary)** | wood, peat, lignite, coal | crude petroleum | natural gas |
| **Derived (secondary)** | coke, charcoal, briquettes | petrol, kerosene, diesel, fuel oil | coal gas, producer gas, water gas, LPG, biogas |

questions.q: The calorific value of a fuel is 8000 kcal/kg. Express it in BTU/lb and kJ/kg.
questions.a:
1 kcal/kg = 1.8 BTU/lb, so CV = $8000 \times 1.8 = 14\,400$ BTU/lb.

1 kcal = 4.184 kJ, so CV = $8000 \times 4.184 = 33\,472$ kJ/kg (≈ 33.5 MJ/kg).

questions.q: 1 kcal/kg is equal to:
questions.a: 1 kcal/kg = 1000 cal / 1000 g = 1 cal/g (and = 1.8 BTU/lb).

questions.q: A good fuel should have:
options: Low calorific value and high ash
Moderate ignition temperature and low moisture
questions.a: Moderate ignition temperature (safe yet easy to light) and low moisture (more heat available) are characteristics of a good fuel.

topics.topic: Comparison of solid, liquid and gaseous fuels
topics.why: A standard 3-5 mark comparison table; examiners want 6-8 points side by side.
topics.gist:
This is a table question. Remember the logic: gases mix best with air, so they burn most completely with least excess air; solids mix worst.

**Solid fuels** (coal, coke, wood): cheap, easy and safe to store and transport, low risk of fire; but high ash, large excess air needed, combustion hard to control or stop, low thermal efficiency, labour for handling and ash disposal, lower CV.

**Liquid fuels** (petrol, diesel, kerosene, fuel oil): higher CV per unit mass, little or no ash, burn with less excess air, combustion easily controlled (start/stop by a valve), can be piped and fed automatically, need less storage space, used in IC engines; but costlier, fire and evaporation risk, need special burners/atomisers, storage tanks must be leak-proof.

**Gaseous fuels** (natural gas, LPG, producer gas, coal gas): mix intimately with air so burn completely with little excess air, no ash or smoke, flame easily controlled, can be preheated using waste heat (regenerative furnaces), piped to the point of use; but highly inflammable (explosion hazard), need large leak-proof storage, and are costlier.
key_points: Excess air needed: solids most, liquids moderate, gases least.
Ash: solids high; liquids and gases negligible.
Control of combustion: difficult for solids, easy for liquids and gases.
Storage/transport: solids easy and safe; liquids need closed tanks; gases need large leak-proof containers.
Fire/explosion risk: solids least, gases most.
Thermal efficiency: solids lowest, gases highest.
Cost per unit heat: generally solids cheapest.
Gases can be preheated with waste heat; used in IC engines liquids and gases only.
traps: Saying gaseous fuels always have the highest calorific value per kg: comparisons are usually on combustion behaviour, not raw CV (and producer gas has a low CV).
Writing a paragraph instead of a table: tables score better here.
topics.asked_as: 'Compare solid, liquid and gaseous fuels' (5 marks); 'Give advantages of gaseous fuels over solid fuels' (3 marks).

questions.q: Compare solid, liquid and gaseous fuels.
questions.a:
| Property | Solid | Liquid | Gaseous |
|---|---|---|---|
| Examples | coal, coke, wood | petrol, diesel, fuel oil | natural gas, LPG, coal gas |
| Calorific value | lowest | higher | high (varies) |
| Excess air for combustion | large | moderate | least |
| Ash and smoke | high ash, smoke | negligible ash | no ash, no smoke |
| Control of combustion | difficult | easy | easiest |
| Thermal efficiency | lowest | higher | highest |
| Storage and transport | easy, safe | closed tanks, pipelines | large leak-proof containers, pipelines |
| Fire/explosion hazard | least | more | highest |
| Cost | cheapest | costlier | costliest (per unit heat, usually) |
| Use in IC engines | not possible | yes | yes |

questions.q: Give four advantages of gaseous fuels over solid fuels.
questions.a:
1. They mix intimately with air and burn completely with very little excess air, giving higher efficiency.
2. No ash or smoke is produced.
3. Combustion can be started, stopped and controlled easily by valves.
4. They can be piped directly to the point of use and preheated by waste heat (regenerative furnaces), giving higher flame temperatures.

questions.q: Why do liquid fuels need less excess air than solid fuels?
questions.a: Liquid fuels are atomised into fine droplets (or vaporised) in burners, so they present a very large surface area to air and mix with it intimately; combustion is therefore nearly complete with a small excess of air. Solid fuel lumps expose only their outer surface, so a large excess of air must be passed to ensure complete combustion of the carbon.

questions.q: State two disadvantages each of liquid and gaseous fuels.
questions.a:
**Liquid**: (1) costlier than solid fuels; (2) fire hazard and evaporation losses, needing closed, leak-proof storage and special atomising burners.

**Gaseous**: (1) highly inflammable, with risk of explosion; (2) require very large storage tanks and leak-proof pipelines, and are costlier.

questions.q: Which fuel requires the least excess air for complete combustion?
questions.a: Gaseous fuels mix with air at the molecular level, so they need the least excess air.

questions.q: Which of the following is an advantage of solid fuels?
options: Low risk of fire during storage and transport
questions.a: Solid fuels are safe and easy to store and transport. The other options describe liquid/gaseous fuels.

topics.topic: Gross and net calorific value by bomb calorimeter
topics.why: Bomb calorimeter (diagram, working, corrections) plus a GCV/NCV numerical is one of the most repeated questions in Indian first-year chemistry papers.
topics.gist:
**Gross (higher) calorific value, GCV/HCV**: total heat liberated when unit mass of fuel is burnt completely and the products are cooled to room temperature, so the steam formed **condenses** and its latent heat is included. **Net (lower) calorific value, NCV/LCV**: heat liberated when the products are allowed to escape, so the latent heat of the water vapour is lost. Each part of H gives 9 parts of water: $\mathrm{H_2 + \tfrac{1}{2}O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}$ (2 g H gives 18 g water). Hence $\mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587$ (H in %, 587 kcal/kg latent heat).

**Bomb calorimeter** (for solids and non-volatile liquids). A strong stainless-steel **bomb** with a gas-tight screw lid carries two electrodes; a small Ni/Pt crucible holds a weighed pellet (about 0.5-1 g) of fuel, touched by a fine **fuse wire**. The bomb is filled with $\mathrm{O_2}$ at about 25 atm and placed in a copper **calorimeter** holding a known mass of water, with an electrical **stirrer** and a **Beckmann thermometer** (reads to 0.01 °C); the calorimeter sits in an air jacket and water jacket to cut heat loss. The initial temperature $t_1$ is noted, the fuel is ignited electrically, and the highest temperature $t_2$ is recorded.

Heat liberated = heat absorbed by water and calorimeter: $x \cdot \mathrm{GCV} = (W + w)(t_2 - t_1)$. For accurate work apply **corrections**: fuse wire ($t_F$), acid formation ($t_A$, $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ formed exothermically from S and N), cotton thread ($t_T$), and **cooling correction** $t_c$ (rate of cooling × time to cool) added to the temperature rise.
key_points: GCV includes latent heat of condensation of steam; NCV = GCV − latent heat of steam formed.
1 part H → 9 parts water; latent heat of steam 587 kcal/kg (some texts 580 kcal/kg or 2454 kJ/kg).
Bomb: stainless steel, $\mathrm{O_2}$ at ~25 atm, crucible, fuse wire, electrodes.
Calorimeter: known mass of water, stirrer, Beckmann thermometer, air and water jackets.
Water equivalent w: mass of water that absorbs the same heat as the calorimeter, bomb, stirrer and thermometer per °C.
Corrections: fuse wire, acid ($\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, $\mathrm{HNO_3}$), cotton thread (subtracted as heat); cooling correction (added to temperature rise).
Bomb calorimeter gives GCV (water condenses inside the bomb).
Gaseous fuels: Junkers / Boys gas calorimeter.
formulas: $\mathrm{GCV} = \dfrac{(W+w)(t_2 - t_1 + t_c) - (t_A + t_F + t_T)}{x}$ — bomb calorimeter with corrections
traps: Using 0.9H instead of 0.09H: mass of water per gram of fuel = 9 × H/100 = 0.09H.
Forgetting to add the water equivalent w to W.
Adding the fuse-wire/acid corrections as heat: they are subtracted (they supplied extra heat).
Subtracting the cooling correction: it is added to the observed temperature rise.
Saying a bomb calorimeter gives NCV: it gives GCV because the steam condenses.
topics.asked_as: 'Describe the determination of calorific value of a solid fuel by bomb calorimeter with a neat diagram' (5-7 marks); 'Differentiate GCV and NCV' (2 marks); numerical on GCV and NCV with/without corrections (3-5 marks).

questions.q: Differentiate between gross and net calorific value. Why is NCV less than GCV?
questions.a:
**GCV (HCV)**: total heat liberated when unit mass/volume of fuel is burnt completely and the products of combustion are cooled to room temperature (15 °C or 60 °F), so the latent heat of the condensing steam is included.

**NCV (LCV)**: net heat liberated when unit mass/volume of fuel is burnt completely and the combustion products are allowed to escape, so the latent heat of the water vapour is not recovered.

Hydrogen in the fuel burns to water ($\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O}$), which escapes as steam in practice; its latent heat is lost, so
$$\mathrm{NCV} = \mathrm{GCV} - 0.09\,H \times 587\ \text{kcal/kg}$$

questions.q: Describe the bomb calorimeter method for determining the calorific value of a solid fuel. Draw a labelled diagram and derive the formula used.
questions.a:
**Apparatus** (draw and label): stainless-steel bomb with screw cap, oxygen valve, two electrodes, Ni crucible holding the fuel pellet, fine Mg/Pt fuse wire; copper calorimeter containing water; electrical stirrer; Beckmann thermometer; air jacket and outer water jacket.

**Procedure**: (1) A weighed quantity $x$ g of fuel (as a pellet) is placed in the crucible and the fuse wire is made to touch it. (2) The bomb is closed and filled with oxygen at about 25 atm. (3) It is placed in the calorimeter containing $W$ g of water; the water is stirred and the initial temperature $t_1$ noted. (4) The fuel is ignited by passing current through the fuse wire. (5) The highest temperature reached, $t_2$, is noted.

**Calculation**: let $w$ = water equivalent of calorimeter, bomb, stirrer and thermometer. Heat liberated by fuel = heat absorbed by water and apparatus:
$$x \times \mathrm{GCV} = (W + w)(t_2 - t_1)$$
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)(t_2-t_1)}{x}\ \text{cal/g}$$

**Corrections**: fuse wire $t_F$, acid $t_A$ (formation of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{HNO_3}$), cotton thread $t_T$, cooling $t_c$:
$$\mathrm{GCV} = \frac{(W+w)(t_2-t_1+t_c) - (t_A+t_F+t_T)}{x}$$

**NCV** = GCV − 0.09 H × 587 cal/g.

questions.q: 0.75 g of a coal sample was burnt in a bomb calorimeter containing 2200 g of water. The water equivalent of the calorimeter is 450 g and the temperature rose by 2.3 °C. The coal contains 6% hydrogen. Calculate the gross and net calorific values (latent heat of steam = 587 cal/g).

1.0 g of coal was burnt in a bomb calorimeter. Mass of water = 2500 g, water equivalent = 500 g, $t_1$ = 25.00 °C, $t_2$ = 27.80 °C, cooling correction = 0.03 °C, acid correction = 50 cal, fuse wire correction = 10 cal, cotton thread correction = 5 cal. Coal has 5% H. Find GCV and NCV.
Why are acid and fuse wire corrections subtracted in the bomb calorimeter calculation?
questions.a: The temperature rise measured includes heat that did not come from burning the fuel: (i) the fuse wire itself burns and gives heat; (ii) S and N of the fuel are oxidised to $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{HNO_3}$ in the high-pressure $\mathrm{O_2}$; these are exothermic reactions that do not happen in ordinary combustion (where S and N leave as $\mathrm{SO_2}$ and $\mathrm{N_2}$). These extra heats are therefore subtracted from the total heat to get the true calorific value of the fuel.

questions.q: The bomb calorimeter measures:
options: Net calorific value of gaseous fuels
Gross calorific value of solid and non-volatile liquid fuels
questions.a: In the closed bomb the steam condenses, so the heat measured is the gross (higher) calorific value; it is used for solids and non-volatile liquids. Gases use Junkers calorimeter.

questions.q: If a fuel contains 10% hydrogen, the mass of water formed per gram of fuel is:
questions.a: Each gram of H gives 9 g water. 1 g fuel has 0.10 g H → 0.90 g water (= 0.09 × H% = 0.09 × 10).

topics.why: Ranking of coal (wood → anthracite) with changing C%, CV, moisture and volatile matter is a regular 3-5 mark question.
topics.gist:
Coal is a fossil fuel formed from plant material buried millions of years ago and slowly altered by heat and pressure in the absence of air (**coalification**). As coalification proceeds, moisture, volatile matter, H, O and N decrease, while carbon content, calorific value and hardness increase. This progression gives the **rank** of coal:

**Wood → Peat → Lignite (brown coal) → Sub-bituminous → Bituminous → Semi-anthracite → Anthracite**

Approximate values (Jain and Jain):
- **Wood**: C about 50%, CV about 4000-4500 kcal/kg.
- **Peat**: C 50-60%, high moisture (up to 90% when fresh), CV about 4000-5400 kcal/kg; first stage, brown fibrous.
- **Lignite**: C 60-70%, moisture 20-60%, CV about 6500-7100 kcal/kg; burns with a long smoky flame; used in thermal power (e.g. Neyveli).
- **Bituminous**: C 80-90%, CV about 8000-8500 kcal/kg; the most common industrial coal; caking bituminous coal is used to make **metallurgical coke**.
- **Anthracite**: C 90-98%, very low volatile matter and moisture, CV about 8650-8700 kcal/kg; hard, burns with short smokeless flame; used in households and steam raising.

**Selection**: for **coke making** (metallurgy) a low-ash, low-S, caking bituminous coal; for **steam raising** in boilers a coal of high CV, moderate volatile matter and low ash, with non-caking behaviour; for **domestic use** anthracite or semi-anthracite (smokeless); for **gas making** a high-volatile bituminous coal; pulverised-coal power plants can use low-grade, high-ash coal.
key_points: Rank order: wood, peat, lignite, sub-bituminous, bituminous, semi-anthracite, anthracite.
Increasing rank: C%, CV, hardness increase; moisture, volatile matter, H, O, N decrease.
Peat: C 50-60%, lowest rank coal; lignite: C 60-70%; bituminous: C 80-90%; anthracite: C 90-98%.
Bituminous (caking) coal is used for metallurgical coke.
Anthracite: highest rank, smokeless, short flame, high CV.
Selection criteria: CV, ash, sulphur, volatile matter, caking property, moisture, cost.
Indian coals are generally high-ash bituminous.
traps: Placing lignite above bituminous in rank.
Saying volatile matter increases with rank: it decreases.
Exact % ranges differ slightly between Jain and Jain and Dara; quote approximate ranges and the trend, which is what earns the marks.
topics.asked_as: 'Classify coal on the basis of rank; give composition and uses of each' (5 marks); 'Which coal is best for coke making / domestic use? Why?' (2-3 marks).

questions.q: Classify coal according to rank. How do carbon content, calorific value, moisture and volatile matter change with rank?
questions.a:
**Order of rank** (increasing): Wood → Peat → Lignite → Sub-bituminous → Bituminous → Semi-anthracite → Anthracite.

| Type | C % | CV (kcal/kg, approx.) | Features |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wood | ~50 | 4000-4500 | parent material |
| Peat | 50-60 | 4000-5400 | fibrous, very high moisture |
| Lignite | 60-70 | 6500-7100 | brown, high moisture, long smoky flame |
| Bituminous | 80-90 | 8000-8500 | black, caking varieties give coke |
| Anthracite | 90-98 | 8650-8700 | hard, lustrous, smokeless short flame |

With increasing rank: **C % and CV increase, hardness increases; moisture, volatile matter, H, O and N decrease.**

questions.q: What type of coal is preferred for (a) metallurgical coke, (b) domestic use? Give reasons.
questions.a:
**(a) Metallurgical coke**: low-ash, low-sulphur **caking bituminous coal**. On heating it softens and fuses to give strong, porous coke; low ash and S are needed so the metal is not contaminated and the blast furnace slag volume stays low.

**(b) Domestic use**: **anthracite** (or semi-anthracite). It has high CV, very low volatile matter, so it burns with a short, smokeless flame, and it ignites slowly so it is safe to store.

questions.q: List the factors considered in selecting coal for a particular use.
questions.a:
1. Calorific value (high).
2. Ash content (low; ash lowers CV and forms clinker).
3. Moisture (low).
4. Volatile matter (moderate for steam raising; high for gas making; low for domestic smokeless burning).
5. Sulphur content (low, for metallurgy and pollution).
6. Caking/coking property (needed for coke making).
7. Size, friability and cost/availability.

questions.q: What is coalification?
questions.a: **Coalification** is the slow conversion of buried plant material (wood) into coal over millions of years under heat and pressure in the absence of air. Moisture and volatile constituents are expelled and the material becomes progressively richer in carbon: wood → peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite.

questions.q: The coal with the highest carbon content and calorific value is:
questions.a: Anthracite is the highest rank coal (C 90-98%, CV about 8650-8700 kcal/kg).

questions.q: As the rank of coal increases from lignite to anthracite, the volatile matter:
questions.a: Volatile matter, moisture, H, O and N decrease while C % and CV increase with rank.

topics.why: Procedure (temperatures, times, crucible) plus significance of each constituent, and a short numerical, is asked in almost every paper.
topics.gist:
**Proximate analysis** determines the percentages of **moisture, volatile matter, ash and fixed carbon** in coal. It is quick, needs only a balance and a furnace, and tells us how the coal will behave in practice.

1. **Moisture**: about 1 g of finely powdered air-dried coal is heated in a silica crucible at **105-110 °C for 1 hour**. Loss in weight = moisture. Moisture lowers the calorific value and wastes heat in evaporating it; it should be low.
2. **Volatile matter (VM)**: the dried sample is heated in a **covered** crucible at **925 ± 20 °C for exactly 7 minutes** in a muffle furnace. Loss in weight = VM. High VM gives a long smoky flame, low CV and much of the heat escapes unburnt; but some VM is needed for easy ignition and for gas making.
3. **Ash**: the residue is heated **uncovered** at **700-750 °C for about 30 minutes** (or until constant weight). Residue = ash. Ash lowers CV, needs disposal, and fuses into **clinker** that blocks air supply.
4. **Fixed carbon** $= 100 - (\%M + \%VM + \%\text{Ash})$. Higher fixed carbon means higher CV; it is the carbon that burns in the solid state and decides the design of the furnace grate.

All percentages are on the original sample mass.
key_points: Moisture: 105-110 °C, 1 hour, loss in weight.
Volatile matter: covered crucible, 925 ± 20 °C, 7 minutes, loss in weight (from moisture-free sample).
Ash: uncovered crucible, 700-750 °C, ~30 min, residue.
Fixed carbon = 100 − (moisture + VM + ash), by difference.
Moisture: lowers CV, wastes heat.
High VM: long smoky flame, low CV; needed for coal gas manufacture.
Ash: lowers CV, clinkering, disposal problems.
High fixed carbon: high CV; good coal has high FC, low M and ash.
traps: Heating for VM in an open crucible: it must be covered (otherwise carbon burns).
Computing VM % on the dried mass instead of the original mass.
Swapping VM (925 °C) and ash (700-750 °C) temperatures.
Calling fixed carbon 'total carbon': fixed carbon excludes carbon in volatile matter.
topics.asked_as: 'What is proximate analysis of coal? Describe its determination and significance' (5 marks); a numerical giving weight losses (3-5 marks); 'Proximate vs ultimate analysis' (3 marks).

questions.q: Describe the proximate analysis of coal and give the significance of each constituent.
questions.a:
Proximate analysis gives % moisture, volatile matter, ash and fixed carbon.

**1. Moisture**: A known weight (about 1 g) of powdered air-dried coal in a silica crucible is heated in an electric oven at 105-110 °C for 1 hour, cooled in a desiccator and weighed.
$\%M = \frac{\text{loss in weight}}{\text{wt of coal}}\times 100$
*Significance*: moisture lowers CV and consumes heat in evaporation; should be low.

**2. Volatile matter**: the dried sample in a **covered** crucible is heated in a muffle furnace at 925 ± 20 °C for exactly 7 minutes.
$\%VM = \frac{\text{loss in weight}}{\text{wt of coal}}\times 100$
*Significance*: high VM gives a long smoky flame and lowers CV; good for gas making.

**3. Ash**: the residue is heated **without lid** at 700-750 °C for ~30 min till constant weight.
$\%\text{Ash} = \frac{\text{wt of residue}}{\text{wt of coal}}\times 100$
*Significance*: ash lowers CV, forms clinkers and needs disposal; should be low.

**4. Fixed carbon** $= 100 - (\%M + \%VM + \%\text{Ash})$.
*Significance*: higher fixed carbon means higher CV; decides furnace design.

questions.q: 2.0 g of coal was heated at 110 °C for 1 hour; the residue weighed 1.88 g. The residue was then heated in a covered crucible at 925 °C for 7 minutes and weighed 1.30 g. A separate 2.0 g sample on complete combustion left 0.16 g ash. Find the proximate analysis.
Why is a high percentage of volatile matter undesirable in coal used in a boiler furnace?
questions.a: Volatile matter escapes as combustible gases soon after heating; much of it leaves unburnt, carrying heat away, so the effective CV falls. It burns with a long, smoky, luminous flame, needing a large combustion space, and causes smoke pollution. Hence coal with moderate VM is preferred for boilers.

questions.q: Why is the crucible covered while determining volatile matter but uncovered while determining ash?
questions.a: For **volatile matter** only the gaseous decomposition products are to be expelled; the lid prevents air from entering, so the fixed carbon does not burn. For **ash**, all the combustible matter must burn away, so the crucible is left open to admit air, and only the incombustible mineral residue remains.

questions.q: In proximate analysis, volatile matter is determined by heating coal at:
options: 925 ± 20 °C for 7 min in a covered crucible
questions.a: VM: covered crucible, 925 ± 20 °C, 7 minutes. Moisture is at 105-110 °C; ash at 700-750 °C open.

questions.q: Fixed carbon in proximate analysis is obtained by:
questions.a: Fixed carbon is not measured directly; it is calculated by difference.

topics.why: Determination of C, H (combustion), N (Kjeldahl), S ($\mathrm{BaSO_4}$) and O by difference, with formulas, is a standard 5-mark question and feeds Dulong numericals.
topics.gist:
**Ultimate analysis** gives the elemental composition: **C, H, N, S, ash and O**. It is used for calculating calorific value (Dulong) and the air needed for combustion.

**Carbon and hydrogen**: about 1-2 g of coal is burnt in a current of dry oxygen in a combustion apparatus. C becomes $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and H becomes $\mathrm{H_2O}$. The gases pass through weighed tubes of **anhydrous $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$** (absorbs water) and then **KOH** (absorbs $\mathrm{CO_2}$). From the increases in weight: $\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2}$ (12 g C gives 44 g) and $\mathrm{H_2 + \tfrac12 O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}$ (2 g H gives 18 g).

**Nitrogen (Kjeldahl's method)**: coal is heated with conc. $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ and $\mathrm{K_2SO_4}$ (catalyst $\mathrm{CuSO_4}$) till clear; N becomes $\mathrm{(NH_4)_2SO_4}$. It is distilled with NaOH; the liberated $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is absorbed in a known volume of standard acid and the unused acid is back-titrated.

**Sulphur**: from the washings of the bomb calorimeter (S becomes sulphate), precipitated with $\mathrm{BaCl_2}$ as $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$, filtered, ignited and weighed (32 g S gives 233 g $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$).

**Ash**: as in proximate analysis. **Oxygen** $= 100 - (\%C + \%H + \%N + \%S + \%\text{Ash})$.

**Significance**: high C and H raise CV; N has no heating value and is undesirable; S gives $\mathrm{SO_2}$ (corrosion, pollution) though it adds a little heat; high O lowers CV (oxygen is already combined with H) and is typical of young coals.
key_points: Ultimate = elemental analysis: C, H, N, S, ash, O.
C and H: combustion in $\mathrm{O_2}$; $\mathrm{H_2O}$ absorbed in anhydrous $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ in KOH.
N: Kjeldahl method, $\mathrm{NH_3}$ absorbed in standard $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$.
S: from bomb washings as $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$.
O: by difference.
High C, H: higher CV; high O lowers CV; N inert; S polluting and corrosive.
Used for Dulong's formula and combustion air calculations.
Proximate analysis is practical/commercial; ultimate is scientific/elemental.
formulas: $\%\,\mathrm{C} = \dfrac{\text{increase in wt of KOH tube} \times 12 \times 100}{44 \times \text{wt of coal}}$
$\%\,\mathrm{H} = \dfrac{\text{increase in wt of } \mathrm{CaCl_2} \text{ tube} \times 2 \times 100}{18 \times \text{wt of coal}}$
$\%\,\mathrm{N} = \dfrac{V_{\text{acid}} \times N_{\text{acid}} \times 1.4}{\text{wt of coal}}$ — V in mL used to neutralise $\mathrm{NH_3}$
traps: Putting KOH before $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$: KOH solution would also absorb water; $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ comes first.
Using 1/9 for H from water without the 100: %H = (wt $\mathrm{H_2O}$ × 2/18 × 100)/wt coal.
In Kjeldahl, using the total acid volume instead of the acid actually neutralised by $\mathrm{NH_3}$.
Using 1.4 without understanding: it is 14 × 100/1000 (meq to g, then %).
topics.asked_as: 'Describe ultimate analysis of coal and its significance' (5 marks); 'Explain Kjeldahl's method for nitrogen' (3 marks); numericals on %C, %H, %N, %S (3-5 marks); 'Differentiate proximate and ultimate analysis' (3 marks).

questions.q: Describe the determination of carbon and hydrogen in coal. Give the formulas used.
questions.a:
About 1-2 g of accurately weighed coal is burnt in a current of dry, $\mathrm{CO_2}$-free oxygen in a combustion tube. C and H are oxidised:
$$\mathrm{C + O_2 \rightarrow CO_2} \qquad \mathrm{H_2 + \tfrac12 O_2 \rightarrow H_2O}$$
The products pass first through a weighed U-tube of **anhydrous $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$**, which absorbs $\mathrm{H_2O}$, and then through a weighed tube of **KOH**, which absorbs $\mathrm{CO_2}$:
$$\mathrm{2KOH + CO_2 \rightarrow K_2CO_3 + H_2O}$$
From the increases in weight:
$$\%\mathrm{C} = \frac{\Delta W_{\mathrm{KOH}}\times 12\times 100}{44\times W_{\text{coal}}} \qquad \%\mathrm{H} = \frac{\Delta W_{\mathrm{CaCl_2}}\times 2\times 100}{18\times W_{\text{coal}}}$$
*Significance*: higher C and H mean higher calorific value.

questions.q: 0.20 g of coal on combustion increased the weight of the KOH tube by 0.55 g and the $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ tube by 0.09 g. Calculate % C and % H.
2.5 g of coal was Kjeldahlised and the ammonia evolved was absorbed in 50 mL of 0.5 N $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$. The excess acid required 40 mL of 0.5 N NaOH. Calculate % N.
questions.a:
Acid taken = 50 mL of 0.5 N; excess acid = 40 mL of 0.5 N (by NaOH).
Acid neutralised by $\mathrm{NH_3}$ = 50 − 40 = 10 mL of 0.5 N.

$$\%\mathrm{N} = \frac{V \times N \times 1.4}{W} = \frac{10 \times 0.5 \times 1.4}{2.5} = 2.8\%$$

(1.4 = 14 g N per equivalent × 100 / 1000 mL.)

questions.q: 1.5 g of coal burnt in a bomb calorimeter; the washings gave 0.175 g of $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$. Calculate % S.
questions.a:
233 g $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ contains 32 g S.
$$\%\mathrm{S} = \frac{0.175\times 32\times 100}{233\times 1.5} = \frac{560}{349.5} = 1.60\%$$

questions.q: Differentiate between proximate and ultimate analysis of coal.
questions.a:
| Proximate analysis | Ultimate analysis |
|---|---|
| Determines moisture, volatile matter, ash, fixed carbon | Determines C, H, N, S, ash, O (elements) |
| Simple, quick; needs balance and furnace | Elaborate; needs combustion train, Kjeldahl, bomb |
| Practical/commercial value: grading and furnace behaviour | Scientific value: CV by Dulong, air needed for combustion |
| FC obtained by difference | O obtained by difference |

questions.q: In ultimate analysis, nitrogen is determined by:
questions.a: Kjeldahl's method converts N to ammonium sulphate, liberates $\mathrm{NH_3}$ with NaOH and estimates it by acid absorption.

questions.q: The water formed in the combustion of coal during ultimate analysis is absorbed in:
questions.a: Anhydrous $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ absorbs water; KOH absorbs $\mathrm{CO_2}$.

topics.why: Occasionally asked as a 2-3 mark short note on advantages and disadvantages.
topics.gist:
**Pulverized coal** is coal ground to a very fine powder (typically about 70-80% passing a 200-mesh sieve, i.e. finer than about 75 μm), dried, and blown with preheated air through burners into the furnace, where it burns almost like a gas in suspension.

Because each tiny particle exposes a huge surface area to air, combustion is rapid and nearly complete.

**Advantages**: complete combustion with little excess air (high thermal efficiency); low-grade, high-ash coals can be used efficiently; combustion is easily controlled and responds quickly to changes in load; no clinker trouble on grates and less labour; furnace can be lit and shut quickly; preheated secondary air can be used. It is the standard firing method in large thermal power stations and cement kilns.

**Disadvantages**: cost of grinding and drying equipment; the fine ash is carried away as **fly ash**, needing electrostatic precipitators; risk of **explosion** in storage and handling (coal dust and air); requires a large combustion chamber; noisy pulverising mills.
key_points: Coal ground fine (~200 mesh), mixed with air and burnt in suspension.
Large surface area gives rapid, almost complete combustion.
Advantages: high efficiency, little excess air, low-grade coal usable, easy control, quick start/stop, no grate.
Disadvantages: grinding cost, fly ash, explosion hazard, large furnace.
Used in thermal power plants and cement rotary kilns.
traps: Saying pulverized coal needs more excess air: it needs less.
Forgetting fly ash and explosion hazard as disadvantages.
topics.asked_as: 'Write a short note on pulverized coal' (3 marks); 'Give advantages of pulverized coal' (2 marks).

questions.q: What is pulverized coal? Give its advantages and disadvantages.
questions.a:
**Pulverized coal** is coal that has been dried and ground to a very fine powder (about 70-80% through a 200-mesh sieve) and is burnt by blowing it with air through burners into the furnace.

**Advantages**:
1. Very large surface area, so combustion is rapid and nearly complete with little excess air; high efficiency.
2. Low-grade, high-ash coal can be burnt efficiently.
3. Combustion is easily controlled; the furnace responds quickly to load changes.
4. No grates or clinker problem; less labour.

**Disadvantages**:
1. High cost of drying and grinding equipment.
2. Ash escapes as fly ash, needing dust collectors.
3. Coal dust-air mixtures can explode.
4. Needs a large combustion chamber.

questions.q: Why does pulverized coal burn more efficiently than lump coal?
questions.a: Pulverising increases the surface area per unit mass enormously, so each particle is in intimate contact with air. Combustion is fast and nearly complete with little excess air, so less heat is lost in flue gases and unburnt carbon, giving higher efficiency.

questions.q: Name two industries where pulverized coal firing is used.
questions.a:
1. Thermal power stations (steam boilers).
2. Cement industry (rotary kilns).
(Also metallurgical furnaces.)

questions.q: State two hazards associated with the use of pulverized coal.
questions.a:
1. **Explosion hazard**: fine coal dust mixed with air can explode on ignition during storage and conveying.
2. **Fly ash pollution**: the fine ash is carried out with flue gases and must be removed by electrostatic precipitators or cyclones.

questions.q: The main reason for the high efficiency of pulverized coal is:
options: Higher calorific value of the coal
Large surface area giving intimate contact with air
questions.a: Pulverising does not change the CV; it increases surface area, so combustion is complete with less excess air.

questions.q: A disadvantage of pulverized coal firing is:
questions.a: Fly ash is the main drawback; the other options are in fact advantages reversed.

topics.why: Paraffinic / naphthenic (asphaltic) / mixed base classification is a 2-3 mark question; it sometimes leads into refining.
topics.gist:
**Petroleum (crude oil)** is a dark, viscous liquid found underground, a complex mixture mainly of hydrocarbons (alkanes, cycloalkanes, aromatics) with small amounts of S, N and O compounds. Approximate composition: C 80-85%, H 10-14%, S 0.1-3.5%, N and O less than 1% each.

Crude oils are classified by the nature of the hydrocarbons in them:

1. **Paraffinic base crude**: mainly saturated straight-chain alkanes (up to about $\mathrm{C_{35}H_{72}}$); on distillation leaves a residue of **paraffin wax**. Example: Pennsylvanian crude. Gives lubricating oils of high viscosity index.
2. **Asphaltic (naphthenic) base crude**: mainly cycloalkanes (naphthenes) with some aromatics; leaves a residue of **asphalt/bitumen**. Example: Californian and Gulf coast crudes.
3. **Mixed base crude**: contains both paraffinic and naphthenic hydrocarbons; leaves both wax and asphalt. Most crudes (Middle East, Indian crudes) are of this type.

After removal of water (Cottrell's electrical dehydrator), sulphur compounds (treatment with CuO) and salts, crude is refined by **fractional distillation** into fractions: uncondensed gases ($\mathrm{C_1}$-$\mathrm{C_4}$), petrol/gasoline ($\mathrm{C_5}$-$\mathrm{C_8}$, 40-120 °C), naphtha, kerosene ($\mathrm{C_{10}}$-$\mathrm{C_{16}}$, 180-250 °C), diesel/gas oil ($\mathrm{C_{15}}$-$\mathrm{C_{18}}$, 250-320 °C), heavy oil and lubricating oils, and residue (asphalt/petroleum coke).
key_points: Crude oil: C 80-85%, H 10-14%, S 0.1-3.5%, small N and O.
Paraffinic base: straight-chain alkanes, residue paraffin wax (Pennsylvanian).
Asphaltic/naphthenic base: cycloalkanes, residue asphalt (Californian).
Mixed base: both; most common.
Refining: removal of water, S, salts, then fractional distillation.
Fractions: gas, petrol (C5-C8), kerosene (C10-C16), diesel (C15-C18), lubricating oil, residue.
traps: Calling naphthenic crude 'aromatic base': it is cycloalkane (naphthene) based; the residue is asphalt.
Mixing up the residues: paraffin wax for paraffinic, asphalt for asphaltic.
topics.asked_as: 'How is petroleum classified?' (2-3 marks); 'Write a short note on refining of petroleum' (5 marks, if refining is taught under this head).

questions.q: Classify petroleum on the basis of its chemical nature.
questions.a:
1. **Paraffinic base crude**: mainly straight-chain saturated hydrocarbons (alkanes); on distillation gives a residue of paraffin wax. E.g. Pennsylvanian crude.
2. **Asphaltic (naphthenic) base crude**: mainly cycloparaffins (naphthenes) with some aromatics; residue is asphalt. E.g. Californian crude.
3. **Mixed base crude**: contains both paraffinic and naphthenic hydrocarbons; residue contains both wax and asphalt. Most crudes are of this type.

questions.q: Give the approximate composition of crude petroleum.
questions.a: C 80-85%, H 10-14%, S 0.1-3.5%, N 0.1-0.5%, O 0.1-0.9%. It is mainly a mixture of alkanes, cycloalkanes and aromatics, with small amounts of sulphur, nitrogen and oxygen compounds, water and salts.

questions.q: Name the main fractions obtained by fractional distillation of crude petroleum with their approximate boiling ranges.
questions.a:
| Fraction | Approx. b.p. range | Carbon atoms |
|---|---|---|
| Uncondensed gases (LPG) | below 30 °C | C1-C4 |
| Petrol (gasoline) | 40-120 °C | C5-C8 |
| Naphtha | 120-180 °C | C9-C10 |
| Kerosene | 180-250 °C | C10-C16 |
| Diesel (gas oil) | 250-320 °C | C15-C18 |
| Heavy oil (lubricating oil, vaseline, wax) | 320-400 °C | C17-C30 |
| Residue | above 400 °C | asphalt, petroleum coke |

questions.q: Why is crude oil desulphurised before refining?
questions.a: Sulphur compounds are corrosive to equipment, give foul smell, poison catalysts in later processes, and on burning form $\mathrm{SO_2}$, which pollutes the air and corrodes engines. Hence they are removed (e.g. by treatment with copper oxide or hydrodesulphurisation).

questions.q: Paraffinic base crude oil on distillation leaves a residue of:
questions.a: Paraffinic crudes leave paraffin wax; asphaltic crudes leave asphalt.

questions.q: Naphthenic (asphaltic) base crude oils consist mainly of:
questions.a: Naphthenes are cycloalkanes; such crudes leave asphalt on distillation.
